## The Apprentice: The Eternal Plot of “Thou Shalt Not Make Unto Thee Any Idol”

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-12 (12 November 2024)
Work: “The Apprentice” is a 2024 film directed by Ali Abbasi.
Tags: biopic, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/uchenik-voskhozhdenie-trampa-2024/

[*The Apprentice*](https://youtu.be/o023dg0Zbgw?si=MAOpVNqTpRSKONyv) is so formal that its main characters remain objects that arouse neither sympathy nor empathy, only the desire to observe from the outside (but for no more than two hours). That is what makes the film good: on either side of a neutral position it is easy to slip into sympathy or antipathy towards the characters, and with active politicians there is a risk of spoiling the whole film. At the same time, do not think the performances are anything other than one better than the next: Trump as played by Sebastian Stan creates a literally documentary effect, and Roy Cohn as played by Jeremy Strong outdoes everyone involved with his naturalness.

But the neutrality of the narration and the documentary-style performances do not provoke the emotional response one might count on before watching: well, at least indignation, say, that personalities like these get their hands on money, or on the contrary inspiration, the motivation to “attack and deny” too, as the characters recommend. Taken as a whole, the picture resembles Ouroboros, the mythical serpent devouring itself from the tail. The ring structure of the plot, combined with the mirroring of the main characters, leads us through one turn of a spiral that will probably never be broken. So watching such a film means getting a slightly better feel for the eternal plot of “thou shalt not make unto thee any idol” (except, perhaps, of yourself)

---

## Twins Played by One Actor: Amura, Gudbay and Vasily

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/bliznetsy-v-rossiyskikh-proektakh/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-11 (11 November 2024)
Tags: Russian cinema, series, list
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/bliznetsy-v-rossiyskikh-proektakh/

**Seeing double…**

… from the number of projects about swapped twins! It feels as if everyone in this country suddenly remembered the film *Shirli-myrli* («Ширли-мырли») (or *Ivan Vasilievich: Back to the Future*) and decided to muse on the theme of twins played by one and the same actor. So I thought about it and wrote down, off the top of my head, 3 fresh projects built around this device:

[*Amura*](https://youtu.be/2cRO3MvDCQU?si=5rTcK7W2t-KSXDFl) («Амура») — a crime action story about twin sisters trying to reunite somewhere between Vladivostok and Japan. The lead is Alena Mikhailova (who got some practice playing this kind of thing in *Kalimba* («Калимба»))

[*Gudbay*](https://youtu.be/UvP1VTh3XpI?si=3yvLPGBdU1Xp8AjO) («Гудбай», “Goodbye”) — a parody sci-fi series about Biden coming to Moscow. This time it is Dmitry Dyuzhev who does the twin duty.

[*Vasily*](https://youtu.be/LXZAnFKEHH8?si=-Oxfmg4m7HwsnE8B) («Василий») — an upcoming comedy about twin brothers: a Russian school teacher of basic life safety (OBZh) and a debtor to a Mexican cartel. Both are played by Alexander Petrov.

Does anyone know what caused this pile-up of twins?) If you have noticed anything else like this, share it in the comments! (I know about *Mickey 17*, but it is not one of ours)

## A Book for November: Ustoychivoe razvitie by Mrshavko Shtapich

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ustoychivoe-razvitie-shtapich/

Tags: books
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ustoychivoe-razvitie-shtapich/

For the birthday of Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service) on 7 November (belated happy birthday to us!) we put together a fresh [shelf of great books from the editorial team.](https://t.me/booksyandex/3725)

I recommend reading the new Mrshavko Shtapich, [*Ustoychivoe razvitie*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/mArXedHL) («Устойчивое развитие», “Sustainable Development”). To my taste as a reader, this text is much clearer and more accessible than his (still wonderful) previous book *Pleylist volontera* («Плейлист волонтера», “The Volunteer’s Playlist”), my impression of which was perhaps slightly blurred by the series adaptation.

In any case, *Ustoychivoe razvitie* is ideal reading for November, the time of year when it is already cold, gloomy and dreary all around, and the celebration of life is still far away. But this state has its own charm too.

## Intermission: On the Courage to Taste the Whole Spectrum of Life’s Emotions

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kanikuly-2023/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-07 (7 November 2024)
Work: “Intermission” is a 2023 film directed by Anna Kuznetsova.
Tags: Russian cinema, drama
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kanikuly-2023/

> - I want to gobble up that mask over there.

> - The sad one or the happy one?
> - Both.

In Russian cinemas from today: [*Intermission*](https://youtu.be/GZ9ORVnK8jg?si=G-BDIysXndwCb6rc) (*Kanikuly*, “Holidays”), the winner of Mayak 2023 (the film festival in Gelendzhik). A film that has absorbed *Sto dney posle detstva* (“One Hundred Days After Childhood”) and *Dozhivyom do ponedelnika* (“We’ll Live Till Monday”), but speaks to the viewer in its own language, which is what makes it worth seeing. Take the quote I put at the top: like the whole film, it is about the courage to taste the whole spectrum of life’s emotions and to accept all the experience you are capable of living through.

In the plot, Tanya, the young head of a drama club, takes her charges, aged 3 to 16, to a children’s theatre competition in Sochi. Going with them to keep an eye on creative types, Tanya above all, is the deputy head teacher Maria Genrikhovna. And although the exposition gives you every impression that Tanya and Maria will be the ones in conflict, the story turns out to be deeper and more many-layered. And where, for the children and teenagers during the 5 days of the trip, the position of the comfortable and worthy adult is taken by Tanya, for Tanya herself that adult becomes Maria. But Maria has no such adult of her own, and that is only one facet of the tragedy of the finale, in which, it seems, nothing fatal has happened.

What I most want to note is the overall mood of the film: down-to-earth naive, recklessly funny. Sleepless nights on the road, the teachers’ humour, maximally uncomfortable but cosy lodgings, an emotional overdose from a contrast shower of feelings: as people now joke on social media, it is “just another Tuesday” on any group trip of a school club, an olympiad team or any other kind of club. I was nostalgic to the full. So *Intermission* really is a small holiday you can immerse yourself in and come out of the film, as they say, 120 minutes older.

---

## Yura Borisov in Crystal Swan: How the Actor Stole the Film from Me

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yura-borisov-khrustal/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-05 (5 November 2024)
Tags: Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yura-borisov-khrustal/

[Here](https://t.me/alperina/20648) [@alperina](https://t.me/alperina) (hopefully in anticipation of an Oscar for Yura Borisov) has launched a flash mob: to tell where and when you first saw this actor and what you thought of him. And I adore telling this story, so I am happily joining in!

Autumn 2018. On a whim, by chance, I go to Darya Zhuk’s film [*Crystal Swan*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/1045133/) (*Khrustal*), about a Minsk DJ who dreams of leaving for America in the 1990s. The film is vivid, distinctive and atmospheric, with a plot that makes you want to hold your breath and not blink while you watch.

And then a secondary, almost insignificant character appears on screen: either a colleague of the heroine’s or her boyfriend, or maybe 2 in 1.  Very soon he vanishes from the screen, but it is already impossible to forget his crazed look and the inimitable body language of a person constantly swaying to a beat only he can hear. He stole the film from me. And it was, as I found out after studying the film’s page on Kinopoisk (Russia’s largest film database, media and streaming service), Yura Borisov!

From that moment I remembered the name and the face and started keeping an eye out for where else this incredible actor would turn up (“well, he must be somewhere else too, he is just walking madness!” I thought). Now he is everywhere, but back then the release of *Bull* (*Byk*; incidentally, surprisingly similar in mood to *Crystal Swan*) was a celebration: at last someone had cast the actor again.

## Crime & Punishment: Ivan Yankovsky Is the Perfect Raskolnikov

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-11-02 (2 November 2024); updated: 2024-12-02
Work: “Crime & Punishment” is a 2024 series directed by Vladimir Mirzoev.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, adaptation
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prestuplenie-i-nakazanie-serial/

## 2 November 2024

Splitting [the series based on *Crime and Punishment*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5377359/) into two parts is an excellent idea.

Not only because it is fashionable in the series world right now (recall *Baby Reindeer*, with its division by meaning, or *Ya znayu, kto tebya ubil* (“I Know Who Killed You”), with literally two blocks of episodes). But also because of the semantic structure of what happens. Today we saw the exposition, the crime (even in the plural), while the punishment, as happens in life, is not only delayed but also more agonising than the crime itself (in our case 6 episodes against 4).

A very simple but effective formal device makes waiting for the second part of the series practically guaranteed. We commit the crime almost playfully together with Raskolnikov and his Devil from Dostoevsky’s metaverse; it seems to fall into our hands of its own accord. But the punishment will come later, when all the thoughts have been thought over, all the hypotheses put forward and all patience exhausted (all the more so given the postponements of the premiere).

There is only one question: how do I now stop seeing this structure in every series I watch along the way?

## 2 December 2024

*\*tag yourself on Monday\**.

It seems Ivan Yankovsky is the perfect Raskolnikov. Misanthropic and merciful, unbalanced and rational, majestic and degraded all at once. His portrayal is especially well suited to the finale that [*Crime & Punishment*](https://youtu.be/RchRWY4waQI?si=xzvvRm0keRfB1SiJ) received in Vladimir Mirzoev’s directorial reading (no spoilers, but the resolution is a curious one).

After watching all 10 episodes of the new *Crime & Punishment*, it becomes obvious that the on-screen madness and devilry around the crime itself are absolutely necessary and appropriate. And just as appropriately they disappear towards the end of the story (or rather jump from Raskolnikov onto Luzhin, Svidrigailov and other characters; incidentally, all the supporting performances are utterly outstanding).

And here a great moment of talentedly deceived expectations arises, leading to an impressive resolution. The series pretends that everything is heading towards what we expect: Raskolnikov and Sonechka off to penal servitude, that sort of thing. But no such luck. And it is for this final surprise, when it would seem nothing is left for sudden twists, that the series is definitely worth watching to the very end.

---

## The Highway: The Poster, the “Spiral of Silence” and a Finale Everyone Decides for Themselves

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/trassa-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-31 (31 October 2024)
Work: “The Highway” is a 2024 series directed by Dushan Gligorov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, thriller
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/trassa-serial/

Halloween is an exquisitely chosen date for the finale of *The Highway* (*Trassa*))

Over 10 episodes the story has established itself as a succession of utterly mind-boggling horrors that befell several characters. So as a horror for the pumpkin feast it is perfect)

But I want to dwell separately on the current poster, which makes the whole content of the project clear at a glance. Here we have the heroine in a stifling noose made of the highway, near which all the madness happens.

On the one hand, clearly, circumstances are strangling the heroine; she is literally risking her life trying to save her daughter. On the other, allow me to turn to media theory (there it is, dear thing, it came in handy in adult life). It has the concept of the “spiral of silence”: a situation in society and the media in which a person is less likely to voice their opinion on an issue if they feel they are in the minority and that retribution or isolation threatens them for that opinion. The silence twists in a spiral through the years, and you get the situation in the series: decades-long abuse of defenceless people by sick freaks. An astonishingly accurate hit with the poster, bravo!

Whether the heroine managed to break the “spiral of silence” and the chain of violence in the finale, each viewer decides for themselves. In my opinion she did not, but it turned out fair, and such a cruel outcome even pleased and surprised me)) Those who have watched it, what do you think of the finale?

---

## An Exhibition About Boris Ryzhy Instead of the Unreleased Film About the Poet

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/vystavka-boris-ryzhiy/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-28 (28 October 2024)
Tags: documentary, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/vystavka-boris-ryzhiy/

You cannot watch the film about Boris Ryzhy (the Yekaterinburg poet of the 1990s), but you can go to the exhibition!

Which is what I did. My impressions were mixed, from a pleasant feeling of recognising the material little things often mentioned in Ryzhy’s poems to a certain boredom, because the curator’s tour of the exhibition is put together in a rather loose and at times even rambling style.

But the exhibition has one special touch: a documentary film about the poet playing non-stop. It was filmed in Yekaterinburg, and Ryzhy’s life is recounted in it by his sister, his father and many other people who knew Boris personally. All in all, atmospheric, touching and informative.

A pleasant pastime for those who are interested in the poet (or who simply want to fill the hole in their heart left by the film that never made it to cinemas)

## Daring: Every Chance of Standing Alongside Brigada

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/likhie-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2025-09-18
Work: “Daring” is a 2024 series directed by Yuri Bykov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/likhie-serial/

## 24 October 2024

The series [*Daring*](https://youtu.be/ZZsPnO0dr4A?si=HgfimuYLnzc-InsK) (*Likhie*, “The Dashing Ones”, a nod to the “dashing 90s”) has every chance of standing alongside *Brigada* (the cult 2002 gangster series) as a saga of equally epochal sweep about crime and the people who are drawn into it (not) of their own will.

*Daring*, as always with Yuri Bykov, sets out the characters’ initial motivation very intelligibly. Artyom Bystrov’s character, Pavel, a simple taiga gamekeeper who makes a living from honey, finds that in 1991 there is nothing to live on, while at the same time his former fellow villager is buying a whole flat in Khabarovsk. A thirst not even for a beautiful life but simply for one that is not humiliating takes hold of the hero, and from then on he is ready to take the word of the fellow villager promising the same “well-paid job”. Naturally, such a job implies nothing good.

The story is very well constructed, made up of two stories developing in parallel, in the present day and in the 1990s. On the one hand, we do not even have to wait 16 episodes to understand where, 30 years later, our protagonist’s son (his main accomplice from the first episodes) has ended up. On the other, the inserts of the present let us not simply watch silently, yet again, the deeds of bygone days in the 1990s, but see the delayed consequences of that time, which now seem invisible. A series I will be watching closely to the end.

## 18 September 2025

The opposition of father and son Likhovtsev in the second episode of the continuation of [*Daring*](https://t.me/kino_voice/893) is constructed as convincingly as possible.

Since the start of the season, only the very worst has been coming out in Zhenka, even if with good intentions (the “help” with his younger brother’s screw-up, for example). The character turns out to be somehow rotten, insincere, two-faced, even by the standards of those around him. Either the psyche of a child immersed in bloody business from childhood could not take it, or he simply absorbed the worst of the atmosphere of his time, but the result is plain to see. I admire Egor Kenzhametov in this role. A curious coincidence that he also played the younger brother of Yura Borisov’s character in the film *Byk* (“The Bull”): in that role Egor, on the contrary, had to stay clear of the harshness of character, while here he goes all out.

In contrast to him, the father, Pavel Likhovtsev, oddly enough, seems brighter. It is astonishing how, with so much blood on his hands, the character managed to preserve (or at any rate to be able to remember) a sincere, bright love for his wife and some sort of value system. Artyom Bystrov’s performance in this role was wonderful from the start, but now it acquires some new importance.

---

## The Alien: Simple Science Fiction That Could Really Have Happened

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/prishelets-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-24 (24 October 2024); updated: 2024-12-24
Work: “The Alien” is a 2024 film directed by Ivan Sosnin.
Tags: Russian cinema, science fiction
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/prishelets-2024/

## 24 October 2024

Yesterday I was at the premiere of Ivan Sosnin’s [*The Alien*](https://youtu.be/REDTP-7B_jU?si=e16bmSzMvAlBXeQa) (*Prishelets*). The film, as always with this director, instils faith in the best and charges you with kindness, and sun and bright colours break through the impassable Russian snows on screen.

Lyosha, a young man (everyone in the village thinks he is strange, but that is not so at all), is impatiently waiting for aliens to arrive: he draws crop circles, tunes the radio equipment in his house, picks up signals and, in general, lives for his idea. In the end he does meet an alien woman, and of course that opens his eyes to life.

The science fiction here is simple, without the tiresome profusion of special effects. It is exactly how an alien might appear in an ordinary village, in the snowy Russian landscapes familiar to us. Such a deliberate avoidance of special effects makes the science fiction sweet, close, inspiring the feeling of a story that could really have happened.

The protagonist, played by Maxim Stoyanov, could not have been any different. It is a wonderful performance, a combination of vulnerability and defencelessness with a righteous anger at a world that promises people like Lyosha nothing good. Stoyanov’s physicality also works for the character: on the outside he looks like a mighty giant, but inside, as we see, he has a very fragile world, which the actor manages to convey. After *The Alien* I looked at this actor with new eyes; that is one of many things to thank the film for.

And also: in Ivan Sosnin’s films even villains get a chance at something better and, without meaning to, set out on the path of good. The film’s finale is proof of that.

In cinemas from today: a warm recommendation to go with your loved ones and share the bright emotions of a worthwhile film.

## 24 December 2024

In my colleagues’ and my [year-end selection of films](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4010434/) at Kinopoisk I, as has become the custom, answered for kindness and talked about [*The Alien*](https://t.me/kino_voice/269). Ivan Sosnin’s new film is striking not so much for its thought about people’s non-acceptance of their neighbour (usual for the exposition of this author’s stories) as for the language chosen to convey this problem:

> In the hands of the kindest Russian director, Ivan Sosnin, the cruel axiom “man is a wolf to man”, to a track by Mujuice, turns into a gentle but intelligible reminder: “man is an alien to man”.

If in 2022’s *Dalyokie blizkie* (“Distant Close Ones”) contact was made on Earth, by driving a few thousand kilometres in a van and talking heart to heart, in 2024 a whole sci-fi with an ambiguous finale is being launched. That is precisely the reason that makes any summing-up of 2024 impossible without *The Alien*, a snowy, chamber story that, in fact, concerns everyone.

---

## Yug and Ira: The Voice-Over as a Lifestyle Podcast About the Hero’s Life

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-21 (21 October 2024)
Tags: series, Russian cinema, analysis
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/yug-i-ira-zakadrovyy-golos/

**How do you make the story of a 14-year-old lad or a 30-year-old single woman interesting?**

(More precisely, the stories of the series *Yug* and *Ira*)

> For those who have not watched them:
>
> *Yug* (“South”), 2024: Ivan Sosnin’s dramedy about a 14-year-old boy who sets off to look for his father all over Russia
>
> *Ira*, 2023: the story of a 30-year-old woman (Ingrid Olerinskaya) whose personal life has not worked out.

Use a voice-over! The screenwriter of both projects, Alim Beschokov, by all appearances, applies this device with pleasure)

In general, a voice-over is used in cinema either as the subjective voice of the hero telling the viewers something himself, or as the objective voice of a third-person narrator who does not take part in the action and comments from the outside.

In *Yug* and *Ira* the voice-over always belongs to the protagonist, which means it shows hidden aspects of their inner world. Literally a non-stop lifestyle podcast about the hero’s life)

The trick is that a voice-over usually voices details left off screen, the things we do not see. But in these series the voice-over often duplicates scenes shown on screen and doubles the effect. For example, in *Yug* there is a scene where the hero goes to buy a new SIM card: we see this on screen. And in voice-over Yug tells us how he went to buy it and why. Visually we see the situation in the third person, but we learn by ear how he lives through it in the first. So the chances of growing close to Ira or Yug become much higher thanks to this device.

---

## A History of Russian Film Festivals: From the 1935 Soviet Film Festival to Kinotavr

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-15 (15 October 2024); updated: 2024-10-30
Tags: festivals, film history
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskikh-kinofestivaley/

## 15 October 2024

All last week I was following Mayak, the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik, and along the way I became interested in the history of the film festival movement in Russia. So please welcome a small (but the first on this channel) **special project about Russian film festivals!** And I have even [written](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/) about the cinema where it all began once before)

Over the next 2 weeks, in a series of 5 posts, I will tell you about the life and death of Russian film festivals from the beginning of the 20th century to the present day, arrange them in order across the calendar year and even try to match them with their Western counterparts by the profile of their programmes.

The first part is coming today!

## 15 October 2024

**1️⃣** **Part ⅕. The second-oldest**

Where did film festivals come from in the first place?
It all began with European film clubs in the 1920s; then came curated screenings with a programme lasting several days, and then, with the arrival of sound film in 1927, the process sped up many times over. So in 1932 the world’s first film festival took place: Venice. It appeared as part of the Venice Biennale, an international art exhibition held since 1893 (the same age as cinema!). There was no competition yet, but at the second festival in 1934 it appeared: the main award was not yet the Golden Lion but the Mussolini Cup (yes, cinema was the most important of the arts for the most varied regimes).

And this is where we arrive at the second-oldest film festival: the Russian one! Or more precisely, the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow. 1935, the Udarnik cinema, an international competition, the opening film *Chapaev*. On the jury: Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, Alexander Dovzhenko. The preconditions for its emergence: political hostility to the regime in Italy at the time and the 15th anniversary of the Soviet film industry, which was celebrated everywhere in January of that same year.

Unfortunately, neither of the first two film festivals flourished for long. Venice went underground for the whole of the Second World War and returned to its flagship status only in 1946. And the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow was never again held in its previous form. Its successor was, and remains today, the Moscow International Film Festival (MIFF). From 1959 it was held every two years, and from 1999 it became annual (who was behind that, by the way, I will cover in one of the next posts). And until 2022 it was the only Russian A-category film festival (that is, accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations on a par with Cannes, Venice, Berlin and a dozen or so other major festivals around the world).

In short, with film festivals everything seems to happen not thanks to, but despite. But when has that ever bothered us?)

In the next part: who made MIFF annual, what is strange about its programme, which festival split off from the Moscow International, and much more.

## 23 October 2024

**2️⃣** **A History of Russian Film Festivals.** **Part ⅖. Changes**

So, [in the previous part](https://t.me/kino_voice/247) we arrived at the moment when MIFF became a regular Soviet film festival held every 2 years. It was an astonishing time, when Federico Fellini, Sophia Loren and Francis Ford Coppola came to the USSR just as they did to Venice and Cannes, and in 1987 the jury president was Robert De Niro. In short, MIFF grew by every measure to truly Hollywood proportions.

And so in 1988 MIFF grew so large that its documentary programme split off, taking shape as a separate (also international!) festival, at that time only of documentary film, Poslanie k cheloveku (“Message to Man”). At the suggestion of the documentary filmmaker Mikhail Litvyakov, the showcase was moved to Leningrad, held there for the first time in 1989, and its symbol (in the first photo) was named the “Kentavryonok”, the little centaur (yes, this image was hovering over the Russian festival movement even before Kinotavr appeared!). Message to Man is still actively held, now including experimental and fiction film and animation too. Kinopoisk has a wonderful [article](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4006929/) with a more detailed history of the showcase and unique photos (I was especially struck by the shot of Leni Riefenstahl receiving an award in 2001)

Meanwhile MIFF began to stall: the collapse of the country, crisis and social upheaval do nobody any good. In 1998 it could not be held at all because of financial problems. In 1999 the post of president of MIFF was taken by Nikita Mikhalkov (something tells me no such post existed before), and since then the festival has been held annually. Let me remind you of the context: in 1999 Mikhalkov is a triumphant figure with *Burnt by the Sun* already behind him (the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film and the Grand Prix of the 47th Cannes Film Festival) and the internationally shot *The Barber of Siberia*. So there is no need to be surprised at the magical disappearance of the financial problems, all the more so since various researchers describe the Mikhalkov of that period as a rather effective manager ([I relied](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/istoriya-rossiyskogo-blokbastera-kniga/), in particular, on the book [*Istoriya rossiyskogo blokbastera*](https://books.yandex.ru/books/JZRDAukA), “A History of the Russian Blockbuster”).

In short, MIFF survived hard times for the second time in its history, but on the horizon other major Russian film festivals had already appeared: Kinotavr and Okno v Evropu (“Window to Europe”). Where they came from and how they differed, in the next part!

## 30 October 2024

**3️⃣ A History of Russian Film Festivals. Part ⅗. Why Kinotavr Is Called That**

So, MIFF survived, and Kinotavr and Window to Europe appeared. Let us look at them in more detail.

Kinotavr did not appear at once. Its prototype, the Festival of Unsold Films, [took place](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/3374283/) in Podolsk in 1989 on the initiative of the businessman (if one may call him that; the man has an interesting biography) Mark Rudinstein. The thing is, in the raging perestroika the amount of auteur cinema rose sharply, but cinemas did not buy it, because the new market economy needed crowd-pleasers rather than art films. So a multitude of films arose that had no chance of reaching cinema screens and audiences. And then Rudinstein stepped in and gave these films and their authors a chance. The authors’ jubilation motivated the businessman so much that he decided to stage a bigger film festival by the sea, in Sochi, of course. Only the unwanted auteur films were not fit for such a scale.

The festival held by the sea in 1991 acquired a programme of two parts: one for audiences (“Cinema for Everyone”) and one for critics (“Cinema for the Chosen”). [They say](https://kinoart.ru/texts/mezhdu-banditami-i-skrepami-kak-rodilsya-kinotavr-etalonnyy-rossiyskiy-kinofestival) that because of this someone joked that it was turning into “some kind of centaur” (*kentavr*). And the film critic Alyona Bokshitskaya corrected: “Kinotavr!”, giving the festival its name. That is how it would exist for the next 30 years, becoming the symbol of a whole film era. By the way, the post of “festival president” (and we remember who holds it at MIFF) appeared precisely at Kinotavr, and it was held by Oleg Ivanovich Yankovsky. It sounds honorary, but it had a thoroughly practical purpose: state sponsorship needed someone whom officials would be happy to receive in their offices and not send away empty-handed. For Kinotavr’s first ten years this scheme with Yankovsky worked, but then something stalled, and the question arose of selling the festival.

In its early days Kinotavr had an international programme (as, in principle, did all the festivals mentioned above). And in 1993 the festival Window to Europe was launched in Vyborg: the oldest national film festival in Russia, focused specifically on Russian cinema. A festival with a surprisingly calm history, it outlived Kinotavr and exists to this day.

In the next part: the rebirth and death of Kinotavr, and lots of film festivals with one-word names

---

## How to Stay Focused: Podcast Volume Slightly Above Normal

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kontsentratsiya-na-rabote/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-14 (14 October 2024)
Tags: notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kontsentratsiya-na-rabote/

**A Monday post: on concentrating on work tasks**

Recently I wondered: why do I listen to podcasts for work louder than music or other content in everyday life? (I do love the hosts’ voices, of course, but not that much)

Because I work with podcasts every day, I can sometimes lose concentration after recordings and listening through other episodes) My way out is to set the volume a little higher than for the ordinary music I listen to. It is still within normal limits, I am not risking going deaf, but at the same time practically all distracting factors drop out of my sensory field: from sounds, obviously, to visual or tactile ones. With the volume turned up, I literally cannot get distracted by anything else.

This seems to be a particular case of the general rule of concentration: remove distractions and unnecessary things from your desk! Only here it comes in a podcast version, for collecting sound edits.

What are your life hacks for staying focused? Come to the comments with your experience, let’s swap notes.

## Anora: A Successful Tragifarce, Remarkable for Its Directness and Simplicity

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/anora-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-10 (10 October 2024)
Work: “Anora” is a 2024 film directed by Sean Baker.
Tags: drama, tragicomedy, American cinema, festival films
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/anora-2024/

[*Anora*,](https://youtu.be/BUtvdzMxw3U?si=GB6RXypwgWxXcMEx) of course, is a film remarkable for its directness and simplicity.

After watching it, the raptures of my colleagues at Mayak (the Russian film festival in Gelendzhik) and at festivals around the world became perfectly clear to me. The film turned out to be a successful tragifarce (albeit one that walks the edge of measure and taste), during which sincere tears stream from your eyes, and yet every now and then you cannot help smirking. And that means a guaranteed emotional response and a conversation on a serious subject where none seemed to be intended. This even though everyone reacts to the film in an entirely individual way, anywhere from boredom to bright hope. As for me, from somewhere around the middle I froze in horror for the heroine, so that not even the solid gangster humour could save me. But it was worth it.

A review with spoilers later; the film is in cinemas from 17 October, and I warmly recommend it.

## El Ruso: A Series About Simple Truths in Complex Argentine Settings

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/el-ruso-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-08 (8 October 2024)
Work: “El Ruso” is a 2024 series directed by Sergey Mokritskiy.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/el-ruso-serial/

The whole of [*El Ruso*](https://youtu.be/fSM0IunUOGI) is out: a series about simple truths in complex Argentine settings.

As I [wrote](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/) after Pilot (the Russian series festival), I was interested in watching the concept of Balabanov’s “city as an evil force” at work, so I switched on the third episode without hesitation. And then the fourth, the fifth, the sixth… And every time the story stopped at a moment after which it was impossible not to keep watching. Not a single boring filler episode. Not a single abandoned storyline. All the little knots tied over the course of the story were untied clearly and in order by the finale, and, what is valuable, not as a soulless cut of each character in turn but as action as distinctive and stirring as the whole series.

The idea of the importance of love and of human treatment of one another against all odds can be framed in different ways. But in the case of *El Ruso*, surrounded by Old Believers’ chintzes and the criminal neon of night streets, it took shape not as a tedious, hackneyed moral but as a skilfully drawn line, triply underlined by the finale. And thanks to the structure (served by the sets, by the performances, which do not overshadow one another, and by certain cinematic conventions) the series draws even those who are usually ready to stop themselves at any second into genuine binge-watching.

It seems this is the case where a series fits in everything, for every taste, without dropping anything along the way. A rarity and a pleasant discovery.

---

## The Most Anticipated Films of Late 2024: Nosferatu, Jackpot, Moana 2

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ozhidaemye-filmy-kontsa-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-10-04 (4 October 2024)
Tags: list, announcements
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ozhidaemye-filmy-kontsa-2024/

I am happy to take up the relay baton from the dear [@Age_of_Cinemaa](https://t.me/Age_of_Cinemaa) (thank you!) and tell you about my top three most anticipated films of the rest of 2024:

[*Nosferatu*](https://youtu.be/2TN9DnF2Yhw?si=0INkfJZ1iOfNi39F)
In general I am not very fond of horror and all the adjacent genres, but here is an exception! Nicholas Hoult looks great surrounded by all sorts of evil spirits; whoever remembers *Warm Bodies* knows: I first noticed the actor precisely in that film about a zombie with a human heart. From the *Nosferatu* remake I expect the old-school spirit of German Expressionism (fortunately, Eggers’s directorial style is in many ways its heir) and an understanding of what problems society has now and whether they differ much from the anxieties of German audiences in 1922.

*Jackpot* (no poster, but with a telling still)
As a devoted fan of *How Viktor “The Garlic” Took Alexey “The Stud” to the Nursing Home* and especially of *In Limbo* by Alexandr Khant, I am awaiting this film perhaps more than any other. All the more so because Kirill Ryabov’s source novel *777* [made a dizzying impression on me](https://t.me/kino_voice/112) as an utterly cinematic text that is simply begging to be put on screen. And from the film I expect, as always with Khant, a story about a person’s borderline state inside our merry chthonic murk.

[*Moana 2*](https://youtu.be/kvDuoTAbDko?si=8CfF95GQr__6vK4Y)
In winter 2023 I watched the first part of the cartoon with delight; I confess I was won over by the villainous crab, voiced in the Russian dub by Ilya Lagutenko of Mumiy Troll (the Russian rock band). I am waiting for the second part to enjoy once again the sweet humour (and moderately black at that: remember how many times the rooster and the piglet nearly got eaten in the first part), the bright tropical colours and the feeling of sea wind in my face)

I pass the baton on to [@kinorevizorr](https://t.me/kinorevizorr), [@kinobloknotik](https://t.me/kinobloknotik) and [@kinokotik](https://t.me/kinokotik).

## Wolfs: When the Wolves Are Fed and the Sheep Are Safe

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-29 (29 September 2024)
Work: “Wolfs” is a 2024 film directed by Jon Watts.
Tags: comedy, crime
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/odinokie-volki-2024/

The film **Wolfs** (released in Russia as *Odinokie volki*, “Lone Wolves”) is the case where, as the Russian saying goes, “the wolves are fed and the sheep are safe”: both in the plot and in terms of the picture’s artistic merits.

An unpretentious comedy about the clash of two criminal fixers in the persons of George Clooney and Brad Pitt shows its ironic tone from the first frames. These peculiar cleaners of the criminal world are at first cramped in the format of a chamber TV play set in a luxury suite, which gives their disagreements an even pettier character. And then (instead of the gun hanging on the wall) the duo is invaded by the revived corpse of a hapless zoomer (played no less brilliantly by Austin Abrams).

And everything in their small night-time adventure is grotesque, hyperbole and exaggeration. The fixers’ industry turns out to be too small, with one nurse, one HR person and one Albanian gang between the two of them; the difference between the generations is declared too vividly, where our zoomer tries to reflect on his feelings while the fixers hurry him for information on the job. That is why the humour works for any audience, and the overly blissful happy ending (our stern wolves let the lad go unharmed) is spoiled, perhaps, only by a crumpled final scene with a meaningful silence. But although I do not like open endings, I am still pleased with the film.

In short, a great thing for an evening, whatever people say about it! If you like this kind of film, I have 2 more recommendations. First, Ilya Naishuller’s film [*Nobody*](https://youtu.be/bZOHmDYCo2I?si=U7jLBklli8ErVW3b), with Bob Odenkirk and no less criminal fun. Second, a Russian analogue: the series [*I snova zdravstvuyte*](https://youtu.be/c1E9atEi7mw?si=iDRjBvpeX20bi2J4) (“Hello Again”, the first 2 seasons). Merzlikin as the fixer, Vlasenko as the zoomer, pleasant humour and bits of Russian reality as a bonus)

---

## A Real Pain: An Unassuming but Insanely Talented Film

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-25 (25 September 2024); updated: 2025-01-10
Work: “A Real Pain” is a 2024 film directed by Jesse Eisenberg.
Tags: drama, tragicomedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/nastoyaschaya-bol-2024/

## 25 September 2024

A promising trailer for the new film [*A Real Pain*](https://youtu.be/b2et8Vpu7Ls?si=goC-lIRZG4KsYfY_): two brothers set off for Poland for their grandmother’s funeral and on the way learn a lot about themselves and each other.

It was written and directed by Jesse Eisenberg with Emma Stone as producer, and I follow everything these actors do with great interest! All the more so as the film has already won the award for best screenplay at Sundance, so now we wait for its premiere in November.

## 10 January 2025

I do not know how your first working day went, but I, whatever that may mean, ended mine by watching Jesse Eisenberg’s *A Real Pain* with Kieran Culkin.

Joking, actually I had been waiting for the film [since the trailer](https://t.me/kino_voice/216). I am always interested in what Eisenberg does, and after the Golden Globes I sped up my viewing: I had to understand what Culkin had done to beat our own Yura Borisov)

In the end I am impressed. I do not remember when I last saw anything as well put together, harmonious and compact as *A Real Pain*. Despite its modest running time of an hour and a half, the film fits in reflections on the subtlety and complexity of family ties, attempts to understand the phenomenon of collective grief/guilt, and the search for a cultural identity from which the heroes were thrown out before they were even born. That sounds rather tragic, but the film is also rich in life-affirming irony, which lets you examine these serious themes without excessive dramatisation.

Culkin and Eisenberg are a treasure in their own right. From the first minute you believe they are brothers, but radically opposite ones. At the same time the declared contrast is not a template but credible, deep and realistic. You believe such people can exist, can be brothers and can turn up somewhere among us. Culkin’s award is completely deserved, and it is gratifying that he got it. The only question is that his role is really a lead rather than a supporting one, but that is another problem.

And the costumes subtly underline the brothers’ evolution during their journey  In the first half of the film Eisenberg’s character prefers a restrained blue, and Culkin’s a rich burgundy. Further on, the difference in their characters is declared: Eisenberg wears an orderly check in the same shade (the character has a steady job, is married and is raising a child), while Culkin wears blurred, chaotic blotches of random shape (he, without spoilers, also leads a rather chaotic life). And in the last minutes of the film the heroes seem to have accepted each other, grown close again and swapped a little of their best qualities, so that Eisenberg is in the rich burgundy and Culkin in the restrained blue. It does not catch the eye, which makes it especially gratifying to discover, like the whole film: unassuming, but insanely talented.

---

By tradition, comparing one with the other is out of place, but combining the two media and getting an expanded picture is definitely worth it. The film lacks the cause-and-effect connections described in the text, and the novel lacks the captivating charm created on screen by Kate Winslet and David Kross. So watching and reading them as a set is just the thing. That is what both the still and the quote from the afterword to the novel are about.

## Love is Evil: A Chamber Dramedy Without Moralising, but with a Cheap Soundtrack

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/lyubov-zla-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-22 (22 September 2024)
Work: “Love is Evil” is a 2024 film directed by Gayk Asatryan, Denis Gulyar.
Tags: Russian cinema, dramedy, rom-com
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/lyubov-zla-2024/

On Saturday evening I was in the mood for what is called a guilty pleasure. I watched the film [*Love is Evil*](https://youtu.be/Qfw-URjc06k?si=4DPxvw-k16aaKLG8) (*Lyubov zla*) with Nikita Kologrivy and Katerina Kovalchuk. I will break it down into pluses and minuses:

👆A chamber atmosphere and a concise plot about a girl who has lost her fiancé but found a friendly burglar in her flat instead.
👆Good humour (with the exception of a few jokes), the pleasant effect of a dramedy without moralising.
👆Interesting performances in the leading roles: the duo of Kologrivy and Kovalchuk looks really great, as does the duo of Sychev and Ardova, the heroine’s parents. And, by the way, the hero develops noticeably over the course of the story.

👇The soundtrack. Not only does it not suit the atmosphere of the story, it also sounds cheap. Apparently, they saved money on it.
👇Rather weak supporting performances. The scenes with the heroine’s girlfriends caused me great suffering.
👇Nikita Kologrivy’s character jokes that he does not bite. Jokes about actors’ biographies are a fun thing, but not when it involves violence against other people that actually happened.

---

## Kombinatsiya: The Story of a Band from the Inside Out

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-09-14 (14 September 2024); updated: 2024-10-26
Work: “Kombinatsiya” is a 2024 series directed by Nikita Vlasov.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, music
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/kombinatsiya-serial/

## 14 September 2024

In the series [*Kombinatsiya*](https://youtu.be/F4R5Et6LW9w?si=yU3aIVrIbDV7kMa7) (“Combination”), about the producer of a cult girl band of the late Soviet years, a lot did not work, as my colleagues write. But I was especially surprised by a malfunction in one particular mechanism.

The friendship of Tanya and Alyona, the band’s singers, is sold to us through exactly the same mechanism as in *The Boy’s Word* with Maratik and Palto (“Coat”), right down to the physical resemblance. Dark-haired Tanya, like Maratik, is a street hooligan and tearaway who unexpectedly comes from a well-off and quite philistine family by late-USSR standards, while fair-haired Alyona is simply Andrey-Palto at the start of the action: for everything good (and musical) and against everything bad. And so they met, went from hatred to love in express mode and found noble friends in each other, which we are supposed to understand from a series of scenes with an exchange of barbs, knowledge (of life or of books, it does not matter) and some displays of female solidarity. A perfect idyll of Palto and Maratik, who practised push-ups, speaking English and singing “Sedaya noch” (“Grey Night”, the Laskovy May hit) and topped it all off with borscht.

And such a mechanism for depicting a nascent friendship is very good: it shows the outstanding traits of both heroes (or both heroines) and helps the viewer warm to and grow attached to them. The girls’ performances as a duo are top-notch too, especially Elizaveta Bazykina’s; she is a sheer pleasure to watch, really! But for me a complete repetition of the mechanics of characters from another series instantly breaks the emotional ties with what is happening on screen and kills the intrigue. And their place is taken by the uncanny valley effect (and sadness at such a confluence of circumstances).

## 20 September 2024

By the third episode of *Kombinatsiya* (very touching and at the same time energising for achievement) I finally understood why the project still appeals to me.

As a viewer with a producer’s background, I am grateful that at last we are shown the story not of singers hired to show their faces and sing lyrics written for them to music written for them, but of the producer who runs all this, and a little of the composer who creatively drives it. These are people without whose work the band really would not have existed, the concerts would not have been organised and Moscow would not have been conquered. Of course, in reality they were and remain off screen, but how pleasant it is, at least in an artistic reimagining, to look at the story of a band from that very inside-out side where Shishinin has to strike deals with everyone and Okorokov has to write the music.

Of course, bands differ, and singers can be the authors and ideologists of a band, but in *Kombinatsiya* the case is different and the priorities in the story are, quite rightly, different. And where we have the wonderful series *Korol i Shut* (“The King and the Jester”), about singers who are also the band’s founders, there should also be a good series about a band with a different background. Thank you, *Kombinatsiya*, for that!

## 26 September 2024

In the new, fourth episode of *Kombinatsiya* there is categorically too little of my favourite character, the composer Vitaly Okorokov, played by Vladimir Kanukhin. In my view, this is the subtlest and deepest figure of all, and every appearance of his on screen is apt and fitting.

On this subject I recommend an [interview](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/media/article/4009440/) by colleagues at Kinopoisk with the actor: it is the most pleasant and calming interview I have ever read!

## 26 October 2024

The finale of *Kombinatsiya*, of course, noticeably adds to the series the ambiguity for which it was already distinguished all along. Behind the grandiose story of the band’s revival after Apina’s departure, the stories of the individual members (except, perhaps, Tatyana Ivanova) get even more lost, and especially that of Shishinin with his sad end.

The last episode, alas, was overtaken by the curse of many final episodes of Russian projects: it turned into a quick cut of resolutions for each storyline. By the list: Apina’s solo career, launched; Ivanova’s crisis, over; Shishinin’s binge, finished; the new band, assembled; the murder, committed. On the other hand, there was a minimum of music-video scenes, which earlier replaced dialogue, plot development and much else besides. And here there simply was not enough time to talk something through, and that, of course, is a noticeable imbalance.

**\*️⃣** But in the end the series still did its job: it gave a little of what I call “angry energy”, when you want to follow the hero and push through any obstacles; it gave aesthetics, because the image really is beautiful; and it gave additions to my playlist, and for that I am grateful.

---

## Yuryev’s Island: The Magic of Cinema in Action

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-25 (25 August 2024)
Work: “Ostrov Yuryeva” is a 2024 film directed by Aleksandr Barshak.
Tags: Russian cinema, festivals, road movie
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ostrov-yureva-2024/

The magic of cinema in action

I am talking about [*Yuryev’s Island*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/film/5451180/) (*Ostrov Yuryeva*): I managed to see it at the premiere screening of the Budem Zhit (“We Shall Live”) film festival, and I honestly had unusually pleasant impressions. In the plot, an unenterprising Muscovite, having celebrated his 32nd birthday, suddenly becomes fixated on the idea that in a past life he was the sailor Yuryev, who almost discovered a new island but died without recording the discovery. The hero heads for Vladivostok by train (yes, it is a road movie), meets a *gopnik* (a street tough) there, and from then on the pals are inseparable on the way to their discovery.

Despite a complete absence of budget (before the screening the creators shared that they had shot the film for 5 years practically for food), the picture is very interesting. Solid craftsmanship comes to the fore, and it creates a feeling of magic. Everything is simply done as it should be, and it works: the actors are convincing, the script, despite the utmost realism, is inventive and generous with unexpected turns, and the direction does not press on the viewer.

Take, for instance, the reflection of the best traditions of Soviet cinema of the Stagnation era: a hero shut up in his inner world and running away from problems, unable to decide on anything, reproachful but loving women (I felt it while watching, rushed to rewatch my Kinopoisk colleagues’ [video essay](https://youtu.be/1aDB1TksfUU?si=VzWODF2mUNkMlRVX) about the era, and was convinced).

Or the Gospel motifs: there is a moment in the film when the hero preaches a sermon to fishermen from a boat, becoming an utterly Christological character.

Also, and this is especially valuable for me, part of the action takes place in Vladivostok, which our filmmakers (for reasons unknown to me) rarely visit, and they should. I have long wanted to visit this city, and that is exactly where I plan to spend my holiday!

And you, if you see it in cinemas or at one-off screenings somewhere, be sure to go.

---

## Morozko: The Opening Credits as the Quintessence of the Story

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/morozko-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-14 (14 August 2024)
Work: “Morozko” is a 2024 series directed by Yulia Lysova.
Tags: series, Russian cinema
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/morozko-serial/

Speaking of credits again. I want to tell you about what is, in my view, the best Russian series of the first half of 2024: [*Morozko*.](https://youtu.be/OXVxBLnxk50?si=3l6Kr99P34ORrUh3)

I will begin my account precisely with the series’ opening credits, because they are, in my opinion, the quintessence of the story. Hypnotic in everything, from the rhythm and the frenzied collage to the music playing behind them, they seem to anticipate each of the series’ features. *Morozko* is:

- A plot based on the real story of the series’ creator, Yulia Lysova: the credits use real photographs, letters and drawings. Yulia, by the way, [wrote](https://t.me/jlisova/1202) on her channel about how it all came together, and there is a lot of interesting material about the series there in general!

- Incredible (really, you will not get bored) plot twists. Everything rushes, races and sometimes glints with neon, like the elements in the credits.

- A feeling of authenticity. You sense that behind every element of the story there is a personal experience, trauma or memory, which Aglaya Tarasova and Nikita Efremov convey brilliantly.

- Harmony of form and content: for example, in the first episode the heroine says that all she has left of her family is photographs, and we immediately see a selection of them in the cool format of the credits

In short, in these credits everything is as in life: something ran past and you did not manage to appreciate it and regret it, while something else lodged in your memory forever, though at the moment it did not seem special. I fell in love with *Morozko* about 30 per cent for them alone)

---

## The Episode-by-Episode Podcast on Games 80: From Launch to Finale

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/poseriynyy-podkast-igry/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-08-04 (4 August 2024); updated: 2024-09-17
Work: “Games 80” is a work  Evgeniy Stychkin.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/poseriynyy-podkast-igry/

## 4 August 2024

I do not write here about my work as often (as I would like to). But today is an exceptional case: under my supervision as producer, an episode-by-episode podcast has launched for the series [*Games 80*,](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883) about the organisation of the 1980 Olympics. And here is a short list of reasons to listen to it, mixed in with some insider details:

- Launching a podcast on the very same day as the series is quite some Olympic Games to organise) In big studio projects, re-edited episodes, changed decisions about how many episodes come out at launch, technical lags and other such treats are not uncommon. And so that nobody would guess any of it, we re-edited the first episode 3 times)

- Already switched it on? Listen closely to the opening jingle: unlike our other podcasts, the music of the episode-by-episode ones is always closely tied to the subject under discussion. You can hear this same melody in one of the first scenes of the first episode of *Games 80*.

- The disclaimer that the hosts watch the episodes no further ahead than the viewers do is the pure truth. What is more, at the time of recording no one on the team knew how the characters’ stories would end. So 0% play-acting in the podcast about *Games 80*! Only sincere film criticism

## 17 September 2024

The episode-by-episode podcast [*Games 80*](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883) that I produced has come to an end (I confess, I love it even a little more than the series itself)). I spent 3 months working with them (in my head, even longer), and here are my favourite moments:

- In the final episode the hosts voice a simply brilliant idea: that Igor is a kind of Forrest Gump of the 1980 Olympics era. It really is so! He saw Brezhnev, and Vysotsky (the Soviet bard and actor) too, he even ended up in Afghanistan: he touched all the good and bad symbols of the era personally, so to speak.

- Alexandra Remizova told a great story about her cameo as Alla Granina (read: Pugacheva, the Soviet pop diva). It turns out she could have got a different role, bigger and more noticeable, but then the project would have been left without the showrunner’s control, which is unacceptable.

- Until episode 7 I thought I was seeing the actress Maria Karpova for the first time and had better remember her. It turns out she transforms so brilliantly from project to project that, having watched the series [*I Know Who Killed You*](https://www.kinopoisk.ru/series/5331465/) with Maria’s prominent role as an investigator, I did not recognise her in *Games 80*! By the way, Grigory Vernik did not recognise Maria straight away on set either, and he tells the story hilariously in [episode 4](https://music.yandex.ru/album/32566883/track/130352481))

- We knew from the inside how the plot of the series would end, but did not know exactly how it would be put on screen visually. I was terribly glad when I saw the funny wedding photo of Igor and Irina: it really livened up the finale and made the standard happy ending a little more unexpected.

## She’s So Cool: Fun, Wild, Absurd, Fresh

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-30 (30 July 2024); updated: 2024-08-19
Work: “She’s So Cool” is a 2024 series directed by Alexander Domogarov Jr..
Tags: series, Russian cinema, comedy
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/ona-takaya-klassnaya-serial/

## 30 July 2024

But the main thing that brightened my Monday evening was a [live broadcast](https://vk.com/kionru?w=wall-203493283_54660) with a screening of the first episode of ***She’s So Cool*** (*Ona takaya klassnaya*), where Lev Zulkarnaev, Denis Prytkov and the screenwriter Kirill Dyshlovoy were present and commented.

On seeing the post about the broadcast, I immediately dropped episode 7 of *House of the Dragon* (honestly!), and I do not regret it: the atmosphere was unique, take a look at my screenshot collage. I learned some wonderful details:

- The *slovo patsana* (“a lad’s word of honour”) that Denis’s hero gives was invented even before the phrase became iconic thanks to the series of the same name (*The Boy’s Word*, the 2023 Russian hit series). Life itself brought this line to life!

- The screenwriter was on set every shooting day, and in film that is a great rarity. Perhaps that is one of the reasons the pilot of the series (as, I hope, the whole of it) came out so vivid

- The script was born from a chance observation in a café: a boy who was having a lesson with a tutor was quite charmingly distracted by a host of more interesting things around him, loudly announcing it to the whole café

- Lev’s hero (according to the actor) is very much like Myshkin from Dostoevsky’s novel *The Idiot*. +1 reason to definitely watch the series

In short, if you are getting ready to watch (I am), be sure to watch the broadcast with the guys, you will get loads of emotions; luckily, it has been [saved](https://vk.com/kionru?w=wall-203493283_54660) in full by our colleagues at Kion, a Russian streaming service (many thanks to them for that!)

## 19 August 2024

The series *She’s So Cool* is over, but it has left many cool moments in my heart! I have gathered my favourite stills:

**\*️⃣** Katya (whose old man is a nutcase with a shotgun) and Batya (“the Old Man”, who is actually Egor) in a little house made of bedsheets discussing a future that never came true. My only regret about the series is that Katya never became part of this story; she and Batya would have made a wonderful couple. I hope that on the way back the guys will meet Katya, and this time she will make a different decision. By the way, the actress Maria Gerasimenko, who played Katya, is simply otherworldly: when she appears on screen, she outshines everyone, no question

**\*️⃣** The trashing of a porn studio in fairy-tale sets and the final demolition of the (fourth) wall. A wonderful full stop to end the series: fun, wild, absurd, fresh, what more do you need?

**\*️⃣** The funny porn producer, angry at everything and everyone, but trying very hard to stay unflappable. He is, of course, an antihero and a caricature, but he did stir a drop of professional solidarity in me as a producer.

**\*️⃣** The guys reciting in chorus “What am I to do I have no money at all put that away what are you doing my mum is in the next room oh god yes”. Well, that is simply some kind of poetry performance!

**\*️⃣** Denis Prytkov’s hero against the backdrop of a Chinese café. The second cool series with him that ends in a Chinese café! (yes, I mean *Kapelnik* (“The Drip”)). I think I know what I will be expecting from the finale of the next story he is in)

---

## The Reconstruction of the Udarnik Cinema: Why It Matters

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-28 (28 July 2024); updated: 2025-03-30
Tags: film history, Moscow, notes
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/rekonstruktsiya-kinoteatra-udarnik/

## 28 July 2024

How nice to see that the Udarnik cinema (a historic Moscow cinema) is actually being renovated as a cinema (judging by the signs on the hoarding), and not as a shopping centre in a Soviet shell! I can hardly wait; it stood abandoned for so many years.

Why does it matter? I have gathered a couple of facts:

- The Udarnik was the first cinema built specifically for screening sound films

- The first Moscow International Film Festival (back then simply the Soviet Film Festival in Moscow) was held precisely at the Udarnik

- The unique domed roof slid open to reveal the sky, but only once: on the cinema’s first day of operation in 1931 (then the mechanism jammed, and the roof never opened again). I want to believe that after the reconstruction it will be opened more than once.

## 30 March 2025

I keep [following](https://t.me/kino_voice/150) the reconstruction of the Udarnik and rejoicing.

Some interesting infographics have appeared, and even renders of what everything will look like and how. The renovated Udarnik will have many screening rooms, a bookshop, a café and, as far as I understand, the famous domed roof in working order (at last!).

The renovation will go on until the end of 2027, so in 2028 it will surely be possible to pick up a couple of tickets there for a screening and stroll around an almost century-old building (construction of the [Udarnik](https://t.me/kino_voice/150) first began in 1928)

---

## Clean: A Plot Backbone Appears from the Third Episode

URL: https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/chistye-serial/
Author: Betsy Isakova
Published: 2024-07-26 (26 July 2024)
Work: “Clean” is a 2024 series directed by Nikolay Khomeriki.
Tags: series, Russian cinema, drama, historical
Translated from Russian with AI assistance; original: https://kinovoice.com/reviews/chistye-serial/

I keep watching *Clean* («Чистые») (as you [remember,](https://kinovoice.com/en/reviews/festival-pilot-2024-izbrannoe/) I am waiting to see what they will shock me with in the finale). And, evidently as a reward for my research diligence, a press box themed around the series has also landed in my lap from Wink (a Russian streaming service)! I will unbox it in a video circle (a round Telegram video message); put 👀 if you are curious to take a look.

It was a controversial move to show us Mark Eydelshteyn, Rinal Mukhametov and Viktoria Isakova in the first episodes and then very quickly get rid of them completely (or almost completely). But the sacrifice was not in vain: from the third episode the story acquires a plot backbone of sorts, intrigue, the right kind of tension, and it is a genuine pleasure to follow.

It is just strange, though, that a series with such ambitions (and not unfounded ones, as you can see by episodes 4–5) started with an extremely aesthetic but not quite substantial slide show of good actors and nothing more. As if there was no faith, or something, that anyone would watch it without a pretty line-up in the shop window (and the scandalous promo as an “erotic thriller”)?

Oh, we will, the plot has really taken off, you just have to sit through to that point first
